title: Cross-Cloud Mapping: AWS, Azure & GCP
interviewAnswer: Map cloud services by responsibility rather than forcing exact equivalents. S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage all provide object storage; ECR, ACR and Artifact Registry store images/artifacts; SageMaker, Azure Machine Learning and Vertex AI cover overlapping managed ML lifecycle capabilities, while container, workflow and observability services differ in boundaries and semantics.
why: Cross-cloud reasoning tests whether you understand architecture well enough to transfer skills without pretending service APIs or operational models are identical.
intuition: Draw the architecture first using provider-neutral boxes—storage, registry, compute, workflow, serving, monitoring and identity—then annotate how each cloud could implement those boxes.
deepDive: Typical conceptual mappings include S3 ↔ Azure Blob Storage ↔ Cloud Storage; ECR ↔ ACR ↔ Artifact Registry; SageMaker ↔ Azure Machine Learning ↔ Vertex AI for overlapping managed ML lifecycle tasks; CloudWatch ↔ Azure Monitor ↔ Cloud Monitoring for observability. Orchestration and serverless/container services do not map cleanly one-to-one: Glue/Step Functions, Data Factory, Dataflow/Workflows, ECS/EKS, AKS, GKE/Cloud Run and related services have different abstractions. Identity, network defaults, quotas, pricing and regional availability also differ.
workedExample: A batch scoring workflow can be described generically as object storage → preprocessing job → versioned model inference → output storage → monitoring. On each cloud, choose services based on team skills, data location, GPU/runtime needs, orchestration complexity and governance rather than translating product names mechanically.
commonMistakes: Saying AWS, Azure and GCP differ only by UI.
Claiming every service has one exact equivalent.
Listing product names without explaining what architectural responsibility each one satisfies.
followUps: How would you map object storage and registries across the three clouds?
When would you choose managed ML versus Kubernetes?
production: Keep data contracts, container interfaces and model metadata portable where useful, but learn the chosen cloud’s native identity, observability, networking, quota and managed-service behavior before operating production workloads.
